title: Why did the little helicopter on Mars stop flying?
blurb: Ingenuity flew 72 times on Mars. Then it crashed. Engineers worked out why, from 100 million miles away, with no one there to see.

cover.alt: The small Ingenuity helicopter standing on reddish Martian ground, with part of the Perseverance rover in front.

source.name: NASA
source.title: NASA Performs First Aircraft Accident Investigation on Another World

cards.b: Ingenuity was a tiny helicopter, about 49 cm tall, that rode to Mars under the Perseverance rover. It was the first aircraft to fly on another planet. It was planned to fly 5 times. It flew 72 times, over almost three years. On its last flight, its blades broke. What went wrong?

Engineers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California, with the company AeroVironment, studied the last flight. Håvard Grip was Ingenuity's first pilot. Teddy Tzanetos was the project manager at the end. MiMi Aung led the project when Ingenuity first flew in 2021. They shared their findings in December 2024.

There was no black box and no one watching. So the team studied the data Ingenuity sent back, and its pictures. Ingenuity found its way with a camera looking down at the ground. It tracked pebbles and bumps, like you watch the road from a bus window. On the last flight, the ground below was smooth sand ripples.

img.alt: A black and white view from above of smooth, wavy sand ripples on Mars, with the helicopter's shadow.

cards.b: About 20 seconds into the flight, the camera could not find enough bumps on the smooth sand to follow. So Ingenuity got its speed wrong. It landed while still sliding sideways, and hit the slope of a ripple hard. It tipped and rolled. All four spinning blades snapped near their tips.

img.alt: A drawing showing the helicopter coming down, hitting a sand slope, tipping over and losing parts of its blades.

cards.b: The team says this is the most likely story, not the only possible one. They had only the helicopter's own data and photos. Other things could have happened too. A later photo from the rover showed a broken piece of blade lying about 15 metres away, which fits their story.

Air on Mars is very thin, about one hundredth as thick as ours. Ingenuity proved a helicopter can still fly there. Now engineers know future helicopters need better ways to see smooth ground. NASA is already planning a bigger Mars helicopter that could carry science tools to places rovers cannot reach.

Lakshmi looks down at a plain white sheet of paper and slides it slowly. Can she tell how fast it moves? Now she draws dots all over it and slides it again. Is it easier to tell? This is why Ingenuity's camera needed bumps and pebbles to follow.

Ingenuity was planned to fly only 5 times. The team kept flying it until it broke. Was that brave, or risky? Farhana says you learn the most by pushing until something fails. Her friend says you should stop while things still work. Which one would you be?
